890.title: The river cut off
890.hook: at Karbala his camp is surrounded and cut off from the Euphrates
890.howItsDone: In Muharram, Shia Muslims remember the thirst of Husayn's camp at Karbala, and some communities set up stalls to offer water and drinks to passersby in memory of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Husayn refuses: a knock at night, a pledge he would not give, and a family setting out across the desert toward Kufa. Your line was: he would not pledge. What small wrong did you say no to? Day eight hundred ninety.

Somewhere on the road to Kufa, the histories say, a troop of horsemen rides up to block Husayn's way. Their commander is al-Hurr. The men have been riding in the heat and they are parched, and so are their horses. Husayn looks at them, and tells his young men to give them water. Give the horses water too. The reports say they filled bowls and held them to the horses' mouths, again and again, until each had drunk. These were the soldiers sent to stop him. A few days later, on a plain by the Euphrates called Karbala, the water would run the other way. Today: the river cut off.
screen: `HORSEMEN BLOCK THE ROAD.` → `GIVE THEM WATER.` → `THE HORSES TOO.`

segments.voice: Kufa does not welcome him. The cousin he sent ahead, Muslim ibn Aqil, has been caught and killed, and the city that wrote all those letters has gone quiet under its new governor, Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad. Husayn is turned aside, and his small camp pitches its tents at Karbala, in the open, near the river. Then a much larger army arrives. And the histories report an order from the governor: put yourselves between Husayn and the water. Do not let them taste a drop. So soldiers line the riverbank. The Euphrates is right there, close enough to see, and the camp, with its children and its women and its old men, cannot reach it. The reports say Husayn's half-brother al-Abbas led a party down to the river by night and fought his way back with some water skins. Shia Muslims remember al-Abbas with deep love as the one who carried water, and the stories of his last attempt are told with great tenderness in Muharram. Keep the detail of the scene in mind: the same camp that had watered its enemies' horses on the road is now refused water by men who have more than enough. The Qur'an says that God made every living thing from water. To cut a family off from a river is to cut at life itself. That is one reason water carries this story in Shia remembrance: a glass offered to a stranger during Muharram can be a memory of Karbala. And it is why the plainest line of this part of the story is also the hardest. They were thirsty.
screen: `KUFA GOES QUIET.` · `TENTS AT KARBALA.` · `BETWEEN HUSAYN AND THE WATER.` · `AL-ABBAS GOES DOWN BY NIGHT.` · then, large: `THEY WERE THIRSTY.`

segments.voice: The practice: drink water thankfully. If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it. Settle, and breathe. Look at it before you drink. Notice how easy it was to get. A tap, a bottle, a few steps. Breathe in. Bring to mind the camp at Karbala, near enough to see the river, unable to reach it. Breathe out. Then drink, slowly, a sip at a time. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you drink and alhamdulillah after. If you don't, just notice each sip. The bell holds the time.
The river cut off. At Karbala, soldiers stood between Husayn's camp and the Euphrates, and a family within sight of water could not drink. Today's word.
Your line: they were thirsty. Today, every time you drink, pause for one breath first. And offer water to someone, even a stranger. Day eight hundred ninety.

891.title: The tenth of Muharram
891.hook: Husayn and his companions and family are killed on the day of Ashura
891.howItsDone: On the tenth of Muharram, Shia Muslims gather to mourn Husayn with elegies and recitations of Karbala; Sunni Muslims honor him too, and Sunni communities keep the Ashura fast that the Prophet kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the river cut off: a camp at Karbala within sight of the Euphrates, and soldiers between them and the water. Your line was: they were thirsty. Did you pause before you drank? Day eight hundred ninety-one.

Before Karbala, the tenth day of Muharram already had a name: Ashura. Bukhari records that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting on that day, remembering how God had saved Moses and his people. The Prophet fasted it too, and asked his followers to fast. So it was a day of rescue, kept with a fast. Then came a morning on a plain beside the Euphrates, and the same day gained a second memory, this one of grief. Today: the tenth of Muharram.
screen: `ASHURA ALREADY HAD A NAME.` → `A DAY OF RESCUE.` → `THEN A SECOND MEMORY.`

segments.voice: The histories tell the morning slowly, and it's right to tell it plainly. Husayn's small band faces the army. One man rides out from the army's ranks and crosses over. It is al-Hurr, the commander who first blocked Husayn's road, and whose horses Husayn had watered. He asks if there is any repentance for him, and fights at Husayn's side. Then, through the day, the companions fall one by one. Then the young men of the family: sons, nephews, brothers. Tradition counts seventy-two in all who died with him. And at the last, Husayn himself, thirsty, is killed. The women and children are taken captive, among them his sister Zaynab, and his son Ali, who was too sick to fight. Sunni and Shia Muslims both honor Husayn. Sunni Muslims honor him as the Prophet's grandson, and Sunni practice keeps the Ashura fast from the Prophet's own example. For Shia Muslims, Husayn is the third Imam, and the tenth is the center of the year's mourning: gatherings, elegies, tears, the story told again so that it is never told for the last time. The Qur'an speaks to those who fall in God's way. In Pickthall's translation: "And call not those who are slain in the way of Allah 'dead.' Nay, they are living, only ye perceive not." Shia tradition reads Karbala in the light of that verse. And so one date carries two memories, a people rescued and a family falling, and both are kept. The tenth day.
screen: `AL-HURR CROSSES OVER.` · `ONE BY ONE, THEN HUSAYN.` · `SUNNI AND SHIA BOTH HONOR HIM.` · `NAY, THEY ARE LIVING.` · then, large: `THE TENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit in silence for them. There's nothing to do in this one, and nothing to fix. Settle, and breathe. Let the names you heard today come and go: al-Hurr, al-Abbas, Zaynab, Husayn. You don't need to feel anything in particular. Just keep them company for a little while, the way people sit with a family after a death. If you pray, you can say, as the Qur'an teaches, we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning. If you don't, just keep the quiet. The bell holds the time.
The tenth of Muharram. Ashura: the day the Prophet fasted for Moses' rescue, and the day Husayn and his companions were killed at Karbala. Today's word.

Your line: the tenth day. Today, keep one quiet minute somewhere ordinary, a car, a queue, a sink, and spend it remembering someone who died for what they would not give up. Day eight hundred ninety-one.

892.title: Zaynab's voice
892.hook: Husayn's sister Zaynab speaks with courage before Yazid in Damascus
892.howItsDone: Shia Muslims retell Zaynab's words in Kufa and Damascus in Muharram gatherings, and her shrine near Damascus is a place of pilgrimage; Sunni Muslims honor her as the Prophet's granddaughter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenth of Muharram: Ashura, a day of rescue that became a day of grief at Karbala. Your line was: the tenth day. Who did you remember in your quiet minute? Day eight hundred ninety-two.

A captive is not expected to speak. She is expected to walk where she is led and to keep her eyes down. This captive had just lost her brothers, her sons and her nephews, and she was being marched from Iraq to Syria. She was Zaynab, daughter of Ali and Fatima, granddaughter of the Prophet, peace be upon him. And when she was brought before the men who held her, she did not stay silent. Today: Zaynab's voice.
screen: `A CAPTIVE ON THE ROAD.` → `BROUGHT BEFORE HER CAPTORS.` → `SHE DID NOT STAY SILENT.`

segments.voice: The first time is in Kufa, before the governor, Ibn Ziyad. The histories say he ordered Husayn's sick son, Ali, to be killed, and Zaynab threw her arms around her nephew and said, if you kill him, kill me with him. The governor let the boy live. Shia accounts add an exchange that is repeated to this day. The governor mocks her: how do you see what God has done to your brother? And she answers, I saw nothing but beauty. Those who tell it hear in her answer that the fallen had chosen their path, and God had honored them. Then Damascus, and the court of Yazid. Al-Tabari tells of a man in the court who asked Yazid to give him one of the captive girls, and the girl clung to Zaynab in terror. Zaynab told him to his face that he had no right to her, and neither did his master. Yazid, angry, said he could do it if he wished. She answered that he could not, unless he left the religion. The girl was not handed over. And a collection of speeches by the writer Ibn Tayfur records a sermon she gave in that court, quoting the Qur'an back at the man on the throne: that evil is the end of those who do evil. Shia Muslims honor Zaynab as the voice of Karbala, the one who carried its story out of captivity so it could not be buried. Sunni Muslims honor her as the Prophet's granddaughter, a woman of patience and strength. And her courage has a particular shape. She did not raise an army. She held a boy, shielded a girl, and spoke.
screen: `IF YOU KILL HIM, KILL ME WITH HIM.` · `I SAW NOTHING BUT BEAUTY.` · `NO RIGHT TO HER.` · `A SERMON IN THE COURT.` · then, large: `ZAYNAB SPOKE.`

segments.voice: The practice: speak truth to power, gently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person with power over you, or over someone near you. A boss, a landlord, an official, a relative everyone tiptoes around. Breathe in. Find one thing that needs to be said to them, plainly and true. Breathe out. Now find the gentlest way to say it, without losing the truth. Zaynab's answers in court were short. Try making yours one sentence. Hold it, ready. The bell holds the time.
Zaynab's voice. Husayn's sister, a captive, who shielded her nephew in Kufa and spoke before Yazid in Damascus, so the story of Karbala was told. Today's word.
Your line: zaynab spoke. Today, say one true thing to someone with more power than you, briefly and kindly, and let it stand. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

893.title: The one who prostrates
893.hook: Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala, leaves prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya
893.howItsDone: Shia Muslims read the supplications of al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the prayers of the fourth Imam, privately and in gatherings, often on particular days and occasions the prayers themselves name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zaynab's voice: a captive who shielded her nephew in Kufa and spoke before Yazid in Damascus. Your line was: zaynab spoke. What true thing did you say, and to whom? Day eight hundred ninety-three.

The boy Zaynab shielded in Kufa lived. He was Ali, Husayn's son, too sick on the day of Karbala to fight, and he grew into a man who went back to Medina. He did not raise an army. He did not make speeches against the palace in Damascus. What people remembered about him was quieter and stranger: how often, and how long, he lay with his forehead on the ground. They gave him names for it. Zayn al-Abidin, the ornament of the worshippers. And al-Sajjad. Today: the one who prostrates.
screen: `THE BOY WHO LIVED.` → `NO ARMY, NO SPEECHES.` → `HIS FOREHEAD ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Al-Sajjad is tied to sujud, the prostration of prayer, when the forehead touches the ground. Tradition explains the name as one who does it again and again: the one of prostrations. For Shia Muslims, Ali Zayn al-Abidin is the fourth Imam. Sunni scholars honored him too; the hadith scholar al-Zuhri, who knew him in Medina, is reported to have praised him warmly. What he left behind is a book of prayers. It is called al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the pages of al-Sajjad, and in Shia tradition it is treasured as words of an Imam addressed to God. Open it and the range is wide. There are prayers for the morning and the evening, for the new moon, for the coming of Ramadan. There is a prayer for his parents, asking that he might be gentle with them and lower his voice before them. There is a prayer for his children. There is a prayer for his neighbors and friends, asking for the grace to visit the sick among them, to give without being asked, to cover their faults. There is even a prayer for the soldiers guarding the frontiers. A man who had lost his father and brothers at Karbala prays for ordinary people's kitchens and doorsteps. Tradition adds a story told about him by Sunni and Shia writers alike. Families in Medina, the story goes, found sacks of bread at their doors by night and never knew from whom. When he died, the bread stopped, and those who washed his body found marks on his back from carrying it. Whatever grief he carried, he turned it into prostration, and into bread.
screen: `SUJUD: THE FOREHEAD ON THE GROUND.` · `THE FOURTH IMAM.` · `PRAYERS FOR PARENTS AND NEIGHBORS.` · `BREAD AT THE DOOR BY NIGHT.` · then, large: `THE ONE OF PROSTRATIONS.`

segments.voice: The practice: read one of his prayers. Translations of the Sahifa can be found online; later today, find one and choose the prayer for parents, or for neighbors. For now, settle, and breathe. Take what his neighbor prayer asks for and hold it: visit the sick, give before being asked, cover a fault instead of exposing it. Breathe in, and bring one neighbor to mind. Breathe out, and ask which of those three you could do for them this week. If you pray, you can bow your head, or put your forehead to the ground. The bell holds the time.
The one who prostrates. Ali Zayn al-Abidin, al-Sajjad, who survived Karbala and left the prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya. Today's word.
Your line: the one of prostrations. Today, do one kindness for a neighbor without letting them know it came from you. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

894.title: Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq
894.hook: Imams of learning in Medina, whose circles, reports say, included Abu Hanifa and Malik
894.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims follow Ja'fari law, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq, and honor al-Baqir and al-Sadiq as the fifth and sixth Imams; Sunni scholars cite reports that pass through them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who prostrates: Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala and left a book of prayers. Your line was: the one of prostrations. What kindness did you do without your name on it? Day eight hundred ninety-four.

A courtyard in Medina. Students sit on the ground in a ring, some with ink and paper, some just listening hard. Questions about prayer, about inheritance, about what a verse means and what a hadith allows. At the center sits a descendant of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Among the people who came to circles like this, the reports say, were two men whose names would later be given to whole schools of Sunni law: Abu Hanifa and Malik. The teachers were a father and son, the son and grandson of Ali Zayn al-Abidin. Today: Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq.
screen: `A RING OF STUDENTS IN MEDINA.` → `ABU HANIFA AND MALIK, REPORTS SAY.` → `A FATHER AND A SON.`

segments.voice: Start with the father, Muhammad, son of Ali Zayn al-Abidin. He is known as al-Baqir. Tradition explains the title as baqir al-ilm, the one who splits knowledge open. A report kept in Shia sources, and in some Sunni ones, says the Prophet told his companion Jabir that he would live to meet a descendant named Muhammad who would split knowledge open, and asked Jabir to give him greetings. The reports say Jabir did, as an old man. For Shia Muslims, al-Baqir is the fifth Imam. Then the son, Ja'far, called al-Sadiq, the truthful. For Shia Muslims he is the sixth Imam, and Twelver Shia law is still called Ja'fari law, after him. But his circle was wide. Sunni hadith collections, including Sahih Muslim, carry reports that pass through him. Abu Hanifa is reported to have learned from him, and Malik is reported to have said that he never saw anyone better than Ja'far in knowledge and devotion. One more thread, as the reports tell it: Ja'far's mother descended from Abu Bakr, and Ja'far is reported to have said that Abu Bakr was his ancestor twice over. So in one Medina courtyard sit threads that Sunni and Shia Muslims would later follow in different directions, and both still honor the teacher at its center. These two did not answer Karbala with swords. They answered with a school. The splitting-open of knowledge.
screen: `AL-BAQIR: THE ONE WHO SPLITS IT OPEN.` · `GREETINGS THROUGH JABIR.` · `AL-SADIQ AND JA'FARI LAW.` · `ABU HANIFA AND MALIK IN THE RING.` · then, large: `THE SPLITTING-OPEN OF KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn from a great teacher. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the best teacher you ever had. Not the most famous: the one who split something open for you. A coach, a grandparent, a professor, a boss, a book. Breathe in, and remember one thing they taught you that is still growing. Breathe out. Then think of one person you could learn from now, someone whose circle you've never sat in. Name what you'd ask them first. The bell holds the time.

895.title: Twelve, seven, five
895.hook: Twelver Shia follow twelve Imams, Isma'ilis a different line after Ja'far, Zaydis another after Ali Zayn al-Abidin
895.howItsDone: Twelver, Isma'ili and Zaydi Shia Muslims each honor their own line of Imams descended from Ali and Fatima; some Isma'ili communities follow a living Imam today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq: a father and son teaching in a Medina courtyard. Your line was: the splitting-open of knowledge. What did you ask, and who answered? Day eight hundred ninety-five.

A family tree has a way of forking. Two brothers, two inheritances, two sets of cousins who each tell the story from their own branch. The Shia line of Imams forked too, more than once, and the forks have names. Outsiders sometimes call them by numbers: Twelvers, Seveners, Fivers. Those nicknames are rough, and the communities have their own names for themselves. But the numbers are a doorway into a question Shia Muslims had to answer more than once: when an Imam dies, which son carries the line? Today's word: twelve.
screen: `A FAMILY TREE FORKS.` → `TWELVERS, SEVENERS, FIVERS.` → `WHICH SON CARRIES THE LINE?`

segments.voice: All three tell their story back through Ali and Fatima, Hasan and Husayn. The first fork comes after Husayn's son Ali Zayn al-Abidin, the one who prostrates. One of his sons, Zayd, rose up in Kufa against the Umayyads and was killed. Those who held that an Imam is any descendant of Hasan or Husayn who stands up openly against injustice followed Zayd's example. They are the Zaydis, and because Zayd comes fifth when the line is counted from Ali, outsiders call them Fivers. Zaydi communities live in Yemen today. Others held that the line had already passed from Zayn al-Abidin to Zayd's brother, Muhammad al-Baqir, and then to Ja'far al-Sadiq. The second fork comes after Ja'far. Some held that the line passed through his son Isma'il and Isma'il's son. They are the Isma'ilis, sometimes called Seveners. Isma'ili communities today have their own branches, and some of them follow a living Imam, present in the world now. Others followed Ja'far's son Musa, called al-Kazim, the one who holds back his anger, and the line went on, father to son, to a twelfth Imam. These are the Twelvers, the Ithna Ashariyya, the Shia of Iran, Iraq, Lebanon and beyond, whose law, as yesterday said, is called Ja'fari. Each line holds that it kept faith with the Prophet's family, peace be upon him. Each has its own scholars, its own prayers, its own sense of what an Imam is. None of them is a footnote to another. Three lines of imams.

896.title: The awaited Imam
896.hook: Twelver Shia hold that the twelfth Imam, al-Mahdi, is in occultation and will return
896.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims hold that the twelfth Imam is alive in occultation; they ask God to hasten his reappearance, and the fifteenth of Sha'ban, remembered as his birthday, is a night of celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve, seven, five: a line of Imams that forked, and Zaydis, Isma'ilis and Twelvers who each follow their own. Your line was: three lines of imams. Which name was new to you? Day eight hundred ninety-six.

In some homes, when a certain name is spoken, people stand, or put a hand on their heart, and say a short phrase asking God to hasten his coming. The name is the Mahdi, the rightly guided one. For Twelver Shia Muslims he is not a figure from a book of prophecies only. He is a person, the twelfth Imam, the son of the eleventh, alive and hidden, and they await his return. Yesterday followed the Twelver line, Imam by Imam, toward a twelfth. Today we meet him. The awaited Imam.
screen: `A NAME, AND PEOPLE STAND.` → `THE RIGHTLY GUIDED ONE.` → `ALIVE, HIDDEN, COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Twelver Shia teaching says this. The eleventh Imam, Hasan al-Askari, had a son, Muhammad. When his father died, the boy was withdrawn from the world by God's will, into what is called the ghaybah, the occultation, the hiddenness. For a time, a few trusted deputies carried his word to the believers; this is called the lesser occultation. Then the last deputy died, and the greater occultation began, which Twelvers hold continues today. The Imam is alive, they say, aware of the world, unseen, and at a time only God knows he will appear, and Jesus will return with him, and together they will set the world right. The word that keeps coming back is justice. A hadith in the collection of Abu Dawud says that even if only a single day of the world remained, God would lengthen it until He sent a man from the Prophet's family, peace be upon him, who would fill the earth with fairness and justice as it had been filled with oppression. Sunni Muslims know that hadith too. In Sunni teaching that accepts these reports, the Mahdi is someone still to come, not the hidden twelfth Imam. So both hope, in different shapes. For Twelvers the hope is very near: an Imam already here, waiting, and believers who try to live as though he might arrive tomorrow. And this ends a week that began with a river cut off: the tenth day, Zaynab's voice, the one who prostrates, the teachers of Medina, three lines of Imams. After so much injustice, it closes on a waiting. Awaiting justice.
screen: `THE SON OF THE ELEVENTH IMAM.` · `GHAYBAH: THE HIDDENNESS.` · `HE WILL FILL THE EARTH WITH JUSTICE.` · `SUNNI TEACHING: STILL TO COME.` · then, large: `AWAITING JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: hold hope for justice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one injustice you know about. Something in the news, or something in your own street. Don't solve it, and don't look away from it either. Breathe in, and let yourself want it to be set right. Breathe out. Then ask one small question: if justice were arriving tomorrow, what would I want to have done today, so I'm ready to meet it? Hold that question gently. The bell holds the time.
The awaited Imam. For Twelver Shia Muslims, the twelfth Imam, al-Mahdi, alive in the hiddenness and coming back to fill the earth with justice. Today's word.
Your line: awaiting justice. Today, do one fair thing you've been putting off, as though justice were arriving tomorrow. Day eight hundred ninety-six.
